title.zh: 鲁迅记范爱农：从东京到绍兴
title.en: Lu Xun Remembers Fan Ainong: From Tokyo to Shaoxing

dek.zh: 在东京的同乡会上，鲁迅认定这个冷言冷语的人可恶至极；多年后在故乡重逢，两人却成了酒友。这是鲁迅对一位旧友的追忆，从清末的刺杀案一直写到辛亥革命前后的绍兴。
dek.en: At a meeting of fellow provincials in Tokyo, Lu Xun decided that this cold-tongued man was the most detestable person alive. Years later they met again in their hometown and became drinking companions. Lu Xun follows this old friend from a late-Qing assassination through the 1911 Revolution in Shaoxing.

intro.zh: 《范爱农》是鲁迅回忆性散文集《朝花夕拾》的最后一篇，作于1926年，这里选录全文。文章从1907年的一桩大案写起：徐锡麟（字伯荪，文中常称“徐伯荪”）在安徽刺杀巡抚恩铭，秋瑾随后在绍兴遇害。徐锡麟是浙江绍兴人，当时鲁迅也是在东京留学的绍兴学生。范爱农是徐锡麟的学生，在同乡会上与鲁迅针锋相对；几年后两人在故乡绍兴重逢，随后经历了辛亥革命。文中的子英、德清、季茀都是鲁迅的朋友，只以称呼出现。之所以选这一篇，是因为鲁迅把自己当年的误会、偏见和惭愧都写了进来。
intro.en: “Fan Ainong” is the last essay in Lu Xun’s memoir collection Dawn Blossoms Plucked at Dusk, written in 1926. It is given here in full. The essay begins with a famous case of 1907: Xu Xilin (courtesy name Bosun, and often called Xu Bosun in the essay) assassinated Enming, the governor of Anhui, and Qiu Jin was executed soon afterwards in Shaoxing. Xu came from Shaoxing in Zhejiang, and Lu Xun was then a Shaoxing student in Tokyo. Fan Ainong, a former student of Xu Xilin, clashes with Lu Xun at a meeting of their fellow provincials; years later the two meet again in Shaoxing and live through the 1911 Revolution. Ziying, Deqing and Jifu, mentioned only by name, are friends of Lu Xun. We chose this piece because Lu Xun writes his own misunderstandings, prejudices and shame into it.

passage.zh: 在东京的客店里，我们大抵一起来就看报。学生所看的多是《朝日新闻》和《读卖新闻》，专爱打听社会上琐事的就看《二六新闻》。一天早晨，辟头就看见一条从中国来的电报，大概是：——
passage.en: At our lodging house in Tokyo, the first thing most of us did on getting up was read the papers. The students mostly read the Asahi Shimbun and the Yomiuri Shimbun; those with a particular taste for society gossip read the Niroku Shinpō. One morning, right at the top, we saw a telegram from China. It ran roughly:—

passage.zh: “安徽巡抚恩铭被Jo Shiki Rin刺杀，刺客就擒。”
passage.en: “Enming, Governor of Anhui, assassinated by Jo Shiki Rin. Assassin captured.”

passage.zh: 大家一怔之后，便容光焕发地互相告语，并且研究这刺客是谁，汉字是怎样三个字。但只要是绍兴人，又不专看教科书的，却早已明白了。这是徐锡麟，他留学回国之后，在做安徽候补道，办着巡警事务，正合于刺杀巡抚的地位。
passage.en: After a moment of shock, everyone's face lit up and they were telling one another the news and trying to work out who this assassin was and which three Chinese characters made up his name. But anyone from Shaoxing who did not read only his textbooks had understood at once. It was Xu Xilin. After returning from his studies abroad he had become an expectant intendant in Anhui and was in charge of the police, just the position from which to assassinate a governor.

passage.zh: 大家接着就预测他将被极刑，家族将被连累。不久，秋瑾姑娘在绍兴被杀的消息也传来了，徐锡麟是被挖了心，给恩铭的亲兵炒食净尽。人心很愤怒。有几个人便秘密地开一个会，筹集川资；这时用得着日本浪人了，撕乌贼鱼下酒，慷慨一通之后，他便登程去接徐伯荪的家属去。
passage.en: Everyone went on to predict that he would be given the extreme penalty and that his family would be implicated. Before long news came that Miss Qiu Jin had been killed in Shaoxing, and that Xu Xilin's heart had been cut out and fried and eaten, every bit of it, by Enming's bodyguards. People were furious. A few of them held a secret meeting and raised money for travelling expenses. This was when a Japanese rōnin came in handy: after tearing up cuttlefish to go with his wine and giving a fervent speech, he set off to fetch Xu Bosun's family.

passage.zh: 照例还有一个同乡会，吊烈士，骂满洲；此后便有人主张打电报到北京，痛斥满政府的无人道。会众即刻分成两派：一派要发电，一派不要发。我是主张发电的，但当我说出之后，即有一种钝滞的声音跟着起来：
passage.en: As usual there was also a meeting of our provincial association, to mourn the martyrs and denounce the Manchus. Afterwards someone proposed sending a telegram to Beijing, condemning the inhumanity of the Manchu government in the strongest terms. The meeting at once split into two factions: one wanted to send the telegram, the other did not. I was in favour of sending it, but as soon as I had said so, a dull, heavy voice followed:

passage.zh: “杀的杀掉了，死的死掉了，还发什么屁电报呢。”
passage.en: “Those who've been killed are killed, those who've died are dead. What's the use of sending some damned telegram?”

passage.zh: 这是一个高大身材，长头发，眼球白多黑少的人，看人总象在渺视。他蹲在席子上，我发言大抵就反对；我早觉得奇怪，注意着他的了，到这时才打听别人：说这话的是谁呢，有那么冷？认识的人告诉我说：他叫范爱农，是徐伯荪的学生。
passage.en: It was a tall man with long hair, the whites of whose eyes showed more than the pupils, so that he always seemed to be looking at people with contempt. He was squatting on the mat and opposed nearly everything I said. I had found this strange for some time and had been keeping an eye on him; only now did I ask someone: who was it who said that, and so coldly? Someone who knew him told me: his name was Fan Ainong, and he was a student of Xu Bosun.

passage.zh: 我非常愤怒了，觉得他简直不是人，自己的先生被杀了，连打一个电报还害怕，于是便坚执地主张要发电，同他争起来。结果是主张发电的居多数，他屈服了。其次要推出人来拟电稿。
passage.en: I was very angry. I felt he was simply not human: his own teacher had been killed, and he was even afraid to send a telegram. So I insisted on sending it, and we argued. In the end the majority was for sending it, and he gave in. The next thing was to nominate someone to draft the telegram.

passage.zh: “何必推举呢？自然是主张发电的人啰﹋﹋。”他说。
passage.en: “Why bother nominating anyone? Naturally it should be whoever wants to send it.” he said.

passage.zh: 我觉得他的话又在针对我，无理，倒也并非无理的。但我便主张这一篇悲壮的文章必须深知烈士生平的人做，因为他比别人关系更密切，心里更悲愤，做出来就一定更动人。于是又争起来。结果是他不做，我也不做，不知谁承认做去了；其次是大家走散，只留下一个拟稿的和一两个干事，等候做好之后去拍发。
passage.en: I felt that his words were again aimed at me. They were unreasonable, and yet not entirely unreasonable. But I then argued that such a solemn and stirring piece must be written by someone who knew the martyr's life well, because he was more closely connected than anyone else and would feel more grief and indignation, so what he wrote would certainly be more moving. So we argued again. The result was that he would not write it, nor would I; I do not know who agreed to do it. Then everyone dispersed, leaving only the drafter and one or two officers to wait until it was finished and then go and send it.

passage.zh: 从此我总觉得这范爱农离奇，而且很可恶。天下可恶的人，当初以为是满人，这时才知道还在其次；第一倒是范爱农。中国不革命则已，要革命，首先就必须将范爱农除去。
passage.en: From then on I always felt that this Fan Ainong was odd, and moreover detestable. I had at first thought the most detestable people in the world were the Manchus; only now did I realise they came second. First was Fan Ainong. If China was not to have a revolution, well and good; but if it was to have one, the first thing to do was get rid of Fan Ainong.

passage.zh: 然而这意见后来似乎逐渐淡薄，到底忘却了，我们从此也没有再见面。直到革命的前一年，我在故乡做教员，大概是春末时候罢，忽然在熟人的客座上看见了一个人，互相熟视了不过两三秒钟，我们便同时说：
passage.en: Yet this opinion seems to have gradually faded later on, and in the end I forgot it. We did not meet again after that. Not until the year before the revolution, when I was teaching in my home town. It was probably late spring, I think, when suddenly, in an acquaintance's reception room, I saw a man. We stared at each other for no more than two or three seconds, and then we both said at the same moment:

passage.zh: “哦哦，你是范爱农！”
passage.en: “Oh, oh, you're Fan Ainong!”

passage.zh: “哦哦，你是鲁迅！”
passage.en: “Oh, oh, you're Lu Xun!”

passage.zh: 不知怎地我们便都笑了起来，是互相的嘲笑和悲哀。他眼睛还是那样，然而奇怪，只这几年，头上却有了白发了，但也许本来就有，我先前没有留心到。他穿着很旧的布马褂，破布鞋，显得很寒素。谈起自己的经历来，他说他后来没有了学费，不能再留学，便回来了。回到故乡之后，又受着轻蔑，排斥，迫害，几乎无地可容。现在是躲在乡下，教着几个小学生糊口。但因为有时觉得很气闷，所以也趁了航船进城来。
passage.en: For some reason we both began to laugh, a laugh of mutual mockery and sorrow. His eyes were still the same, but strangely, in just these few years, white hair had appeared on his head, though perhaps it had been there all along and I had not noticed it before. He wore a very old cloth riding jacket and worn-out cloth shoes, and looked very poor. Speaking of what had happened to him, he said that later he had run out of money for his studies and could not continue abroad, so he had come back. After returning home he had met with contempt, exclusion and persecution, until there was almost no place for him. Now he was hiding in the country, teaching a few primary-school pupils to make a living. But because he sometimes felt stifled, he would also take the passenger boat into town.

passage.zh: 他又告诉我现在爱喝酒，于是我们便喝酒。从此他每一进城，必定来访我，非常相熟了。我们醉后常谈些愚不可及的疯话，连母亲偶然听到了也发笑。一天我忽而记起在东京开同乡会时的旧事，便问他：
passage.en: He also told me that he liked drinking now, so we drank. From then on, every time he came into town he was sure to call on me, and we became very familiar. When drunk we often talked unbelievably foolish, crazy nonsense, so that even my mother laughed when she happened to overhear. One day I suddenly remembered the old business of the provincial association meeting in Tokyo, and asked him:

passage.zh: “那一天你专门反对我，而且故意似的，究竟是什么缘故呢？”
passage.en: “That day you opposed me at every turn, and as if on purpose. What was the reason, really?”

passage.zh: “你还不知道？我一向就讨厌你的，——不但我，我们。”
passage.en: “You still don't know? I'd always disliked you,—not just me, all of us.”

passage.zh: “你那时之前，早知道我是谁么？”
passage.en: “Did you know who I was before that, then?”

passage.zh: “怎么不知道。我们到横滨，来接的不就是子英和你么？你看不起我们，摇摇头，你自己还记得么？”
passage.en: “How could I not? When we arrived at Yokohama, weren't the people who came to meet us Ziying and you? You looked down on us and shook your head. Do you remember that yourself?”

passage.zh: 我略略一想，记得的，虽然是七八年前的事。那时是子英来约我的，说到横滨去接新来留学的同乡。汽船一到，看见一大堆，大概一共有十多人，一上岸便将行李放到税关上去候查检，关吏在衣箱中翻来翻去，忽然翻出一双绣花的弓鞋来，便放下公事，拿着子细地看。我很不满，心里想，这些鸟男人，怎么带这东西来呢。自己不注意，那时也许就摇了摇头。检验完毕，在客店小坐之后，即须上火车。不料这一群读书人又在客车上让起坐位来了，甲要乙坐在这位上，乙要丙去坐，揖让未终，火车已开，车身一摇，即刻跌倒了三四个。我那时也很不满，暗地里想：连火车上的坐位，他们也要分出尊卑来……。自己不注意，也许又摇了摇头。然而那群雍容揖让的人物中就有范爱农，却直到这一天才想到。岂但他呢，说起来也惭愧，这一群里，还有后来在安徽战死的陈伯平烈士，被害的马宗汉烈士；被囚在黑狱里，到革命后才见天日而身上永带着匪刑的伤痕的也还有一两人。而我都茫无所知，摇着头将他们一并运上东京了。徐伯荪虽然和他们同船来，却不在这车上，因为他在神户就和他的夫人坐车走了陆路了。
passage.en: I thought for a moment and did remember, though it had been seven or eight years before. Ziying had come to ask me to go with him to Yokohama to meet some fellow provincials newly arrived to study. When the steamer came in we saw a big crowd, probably more than ten people altogether. As soon as they landed they put their luggage at the customs house to wait for inspection. The customs officer was rummaging back and forth in a clothes trunk when he suddenly turned up a pair of embroidered shoes for bound feet; he put aside his official business and held them up to examine them closely. I was very displeased and thought to myself, why on earth would these damned men bring such things? Without noticing, I may have shaken my head then. When the inspection was over, after sitting for a while at an inn, we had to board the train. Unexpectedly, this crowd of scholars began deferring to one another over the seats in the carriage: A wanted B to take this seat, B wanted C to sit there, and before the bowing and yielding was over the train started, the carriage lurched, and three or four of them fell over at once. I was very displeased then too, and thought privately: even over seats on a train they have to sort out who is senior and who is junior…. Without noticing, I may have shaken my head again. Yet among those dignified, bowing, yielding figures was Fan Ainong, and I had not realised it until this day. And not only him; it is shameful to say, but in that group there were also the martyr Chen Boping, who later died fighting in Anhui, and the martyr Ma Zonghan, who was put to death; and there were also one or two who were imprisoned in dark jails and saw the light of day only after the revolution, bearing for ever on their bodies the scars of savage torture. And I knew nothing of any of this, and shaking my head, shipped them all off together to Tokyo. Xu Bosun had come on the same boat as they had, but he was not on that train, because at Kobe he and his wife had gone on by land.

passage.zh: 我想我那时摇头大约有两回，他们看见的不知道是那一回。让坐时喧闹，检查时幽静，一定是在税关上的那一回了，试问爱农，果然是的。
passage.en: I think I probably shook my head twice then; I did not know which time they had seen. While they were giving up their seats it was noisy, while their luggage was being inspected it was quiet, so it must have been the time at the customs house. I asked Ainong, and so it was.

passage.zh: “我真不懂你们带这东西做什么？是谁的？”
passage.en: “I really don't understand why you brought those things. Whose were they?”

passage.zh: “还不是我们师母的？”他瞪着他多白的眼。
passage.en: “Whose do you think? Our teacher's wife's, of course.” He glared at me with his eyes that were mostly white.

passage.zh: “到东京就要假装大脚，又何必带这东西呢？”
passage.en: “When she got to Tokyo she would have to pretend to have big feet anyway, so why bring those things?”

passage.zh: “谁知道呢？你问她去。”
passage.en: “Who knows? Go and ask her.”

passage.zh: 到冬初，我们的景况更拮据了，然而还喝酒，讲笑话。忽然是武昌起义，接着是绍兴光复。第二天爱农就上城来，戴着农夫常用的毡帽，那笑容是从来没有见过的。
passage.en: By early winter our circumstances were even more straitened, but we still drank and told jokes. Suddenly came the Wuchang Uprising, and then the restoration of Shaoxing. The next day Ainong came into town, wearing the felt hat that peasants usually wear, with a smile I had never seen before.

passage.zh: “老迅，我们今天不喝酒了。我要去看看光复的绍兴。我们同去。”
passage.en: “Old Xun, we won't drink today. I want to go and see Shaoxing restored. Let's go together.”

passage.zh: 我们便到街上去走了一通，满眼是白旗。然而貌虽如此，内骨子是依旧的，因为还是几个旧乡绅所组织的军政府，什么铁路股东是行政司长，钱店掌柜是军械司长……。这军政府也到底不长久，几个少年一嚷，王金发带兵从杭州进来了，但即使不嚷或者也会来。他进来以后，也就被许多闲汉和新进的革命党所包围，大做王都督。在衙门里的人物，穿布衣来的，不上十天也大概换上皮袍子了，天气还并不冷。
passage.en: So we went for a walk through the streets. White flags everywhere. But though it looked like this, underneath it was the same as before, because it was still a military government organised by a few of the old gentry: some railway shareholder was head of administration, a money-shop manager was head of ordnance…. This military government did not last long in the end. A few young men made a clamour, and Wang Jinfa came in with troops from Hangzhou; though even without the clamour he might perhaps have come. After he came in, he too was surrounded by a lot of idlers and new members of the revolutionary party, and set about being Military Governor Wang in grand style. Of the men in the yamen, those who had arrived in cotton clothes had mostly changed into fur gowns within ten days, though the weather was not yet cold.

passage.zh: 我被摆在师范学校校长的饭碗旁边，王都督给了我校款二百元。爱农做监学，还是那件布袍子，但不大喝酒了，也很少有工夫谈闲天。他办事，兼教书，实在勤快得可以。
passage.en: I was set down beside the rice bowl of principal of the normal school, and Governor Wang gave me two hundred dollars for school funds. Ainong became the school supervisor, still in that cotton gown, but he did not drink much any more and seldom had time for idle chatter. He handled the administration and taught as well, and was really diligent to a remarkable degree.

passage.zh: “情形还是不行，王金发他们。”一个去年听过我的讲义的少年来访我，慷慨地说，“我们要办一种报来监督他们。不过发起人要借用先生的名字。还有一个是子英先生，一个是德清先生。为社会，我们知道你决不推却的。”
passage.en: “Things are still no good, Wang Jinfa and his lot.” A young man who had attended my lectures the year before came to see me and said fervently, “We want to start a newspaper to keep an eye on them. But we'd like to borrow your name as one of the founders. Another is Mr Ziying, and another Mr Deqing. For the sake of society, we know you certainly won't refuse.”

passage.zh: 我答应他了。两天后便看见出报的传单，发起人诚然是三个。五天后便见报，开首便骂军政府和那里面的人员；此后是骂都督、都督的亲戚、同乡、姨太太……。
passage.en: I agreed. Two days later I saw the handbill announcing the paper, and there were indeed three founders. Five days later the paper appeared. It began by attacking the military government and the people in it; after that it attacked the governor, the governor's relatives, his fellow townsmen, his concubines….

passage.zh: 这样地骂了十多天，就有一种消息传到我的家里来，说都督因为你们诈取了他的钱，还骂他，要派人用手枪来打死你们了。
passage.en: After a dozen or so days of attacks like this, a rumour reached my home: it was said that because you people had swindled money out of him and were still attacking him, the governor was going to send men with pistols to shoot you dead.

passage.zh: 别人倒还不打紧，第一个着急的是我的母亲，叮嘱我不要再出去。但我还是照常走，并且说明，王金发是不来打死我们的，他虽然绿林大学出身，而杀人却不很轻易。况且我拿的是校款，这一点他还能明白的，不过说说罢了。
passage.en: The others did not much mind, but the first to worry was my mother, who urged me not to go out any more. But I went about as usual, and explained that Wang Jinfa was not going to come and shoot us; although he was a graduate of the University of the Greenwood, he did not kill people very lightly. Besides, what I had taken was school funds; he could understand that much. It was just talk.

passage.zh: 果然没有来杀。写信去要经费，又取了二百元。但仿佛有些怒意，同时传令道：再来要，没有了！
passage.en: Sure enough, no one came to kill us. I wrote asking for funds and got another two hundred dollars. But he seemed somewhat angry, and at the same time sent word: if you come asking again, there's no more!

passage.zh: 不过爱农得到了一种新消息，却使我很为难。原来所谓“诈取”者，并非指学校经费而言，是指另有送给报馆的一笔款。报纸上骂了几天之后，王金发便叫人送去了五百元。于是乎我们的少年们便开起会议来，第一个问题是：收不收？决议曰：收。第二个问题是：收了之后骂不骂？决议曰：骂。理由是：收钱之后，他是股东；股东不好，自然要骂。
passage.en: But Ainong had got hold of a new piece of news which put me in a very awkward position. It turned out that the so-called “swindling” did not refer to the school funds but to another sum, sent to the newspaper office. After the paper had attacked him for a few days, Wang Jinfa had sent someone round with five hundred dollars. And so our young men held a meeting. The first question was: accept it or not? Resolved: accept. The second question was: after accepting it, attack him or not? Resolved: attack. The reason: once we have his money, he is a shareholder; if a shareholder behaves badly, naturally he must be attacked.

passage.zh: 我即刻到报馆去问这事的真假。都是真的。略说了几句不该收他钱的话，一个名为会计的便不高兴了，质问我道：
passage.en: I went straight to the newspaper office to ask whether this was true. It was all true. When I said a few words about how they ought not to have taken his money, a man who was called the accountant took offence and demanded of me:

passage.zh: “报馆为什么不收股本？”
passage.en: “Why shouldn't a newspaper accept share capital?”

passage.zh: “这不是股本……。”
passage.en: “This isn't share capital….”

passage.zh: “不是股本是什么？”
passage.en: “If it's not share capital, what is it?”

passage.zh: 我就不再说下去了，这一点世故是早已知道的，倘我再说出连累我们的话来，他就会面斥我太爱惜不值钱的生命，不肯为社会牺牲，或者明天在报上就可以看见我怎样怕死发抖的记载。
passage.en: I said no more. I had long known this much of the ways of the world: if I went on to say anything about it getting us into trouble, he would rebuke me to my face for caring too much about my worthless life and being unwilling to sacrifice myself for society, or the next day I might read in the paper an account of how I trembled in fear of death.

passage.zh: 然而事情很凑巧，季茀写信来催我往南京了。爱农也很赞成，但颇凄凉，说：——
passage.en: But as luck would have it, Jifu wrote urging me to come to Nanjing. Ainong was all for it too, but said, rather sadly:—

passage.zh: “这里又是那样，住不得。你快去罢……。”
passage.en: “It's like that here again; you can't stay. You'd better go quickly….”

passage.zh: 我懂得他无声的话，决计往南京。先到都督府去辞职，自然照准，派来了一个拖鼻涕的接收员，我交出账目和余款一角又两铜元，不是校长了。后任是孔教会会长傅力臣。
passage.en: I understood what he left unsaid, and decided to go to Nanjing. First I went to the governor's office to resign, which was of course approved, and a snot-nosed official was sent to take over. I handed over the accounts and the remaining funds of ten cents and two coppers, and was no longer principal. My successor was Fu Lichen, president of the Confucian Society.

passage.zh: 报馆案是我到南京后两三个星期了结的，被一群兵们捣毁。子英在乡下，没有事；德清适值在城里，大腿上被刺了一尖刀。他大怒了。自然，这是很有些痛的，怪他不得。他大怒之后，脱下衣服，照了一张照片，以显示一寸来宽的刀伤，并且做一篇文章叙述情形，向各处分送，宣传军政府的横暴。我想，这种照片现在是大约未必还有人收藏着了，尺寸太小，刀伤缩小到几乎等于无，如果不加说明，看见的人一定以为是带些疯气的风流人物的裸体照片，倘遇见孙传芳大帅，还怕要被禁止的。
passage.en: The newspaper affair was settled two or three weeks after I got to Nanjing: the office was smashed up by a band of soldiers. Ziying was in the country and came to no harm; Deqing happened to be in town and was stabbed in the thigh with a sharp knife. He was furious. Naturally, it was rather painful; one could not blame him. After his fury, he took off his clothes and had a photograph taken to show the knife wound, about an inch wide, and he wrote an article describing what had happened and sent it round everywhere, to publicise the brutality of the military government. I imagine hardly anyone still keeps such a photograph now. It was too small; the knife wound shrank to almost nothing, and without an explanation anyone who saw it would surely take it for a nude photograph of some romantic with a touch of madness. Should it come to the notice of Marshal Sun Chuanfang, I fear it would be banned.

passage.zh: 我从南京移到北京的时候，爱农的学监也被孔教会会长的校长设法去掉了。他又成了革命前的爱农。我想为他在北京寻一点小事做，这是他非常希望的，然而没有机会。他后来便到一个熟人的家里去寄食，也时时给我信，景况愈困穷，言辞也愈凄苦。终于又非走出这熟人的家不可，便在各处飘浮。不久，忽然从同乡那里得到一个消息，说他已经掉在水里，淹死了。
passage.en: By the time I moved from Nanjing to Beijing, Ainong's post as supervisor had also been got rid of by the principal who was president of the Confucian Society. He became again the Ainong of before the revolution. I wanted to find some small job for him in Beijing, which he very much hoped for, but there was no opportunity. Later he went to live off an acquaintance's family, and often wrote to me; the poorer his circumstances became, the more bitter his words. In the end he had to leave this acquaintance's house too, and drifted from place to place. Before long, suddenly, I heard from a fellow townsman that he had fallen into the water and drowned.

passage.zh: 我疑心他是自杀。因为他是浮水的好手，不容易淹死的。
passage.en: I suspected he had killed himself. For he was a fine swimmer and would not easily drown.

passage.zh: 夜间独坐在会馆里，十分悲凉，又疑心这消息并不确，但无端又觉得这是极其可靠的，虽然并无证据。一点法子都没有，只做了四首诗，后来曾在一种日报上发表，现在是将要忘记完了。只记得一首里的六句，起首四句是：“把酒论天下，先生小酒人，大圜犹酩酊，微醉合沉沦。”中间忘掉两句，末了是“旧朋云散尽，余亦等轻尘。”
passage.en: Sitting alone at night in the guild hall, I felt deeply desolate, and again suspected the news was not true; yet for no reason I also felt it was absolutely reliable, though there was no evidence. There was nothing at all to be done; I only wrote four poems, which were later published in some daily paper, and which by now I have almost entirely forgotten. I remember only six lines of one, the first four being: “Over wine we discussed the world; you, sir, made light of drink. The great globe is still dead drunk; a little tipsy, you were bound to sink.” I have forgotten the two lines in the middle; the last were “Old friends have scattered like the clouds, and I too am no more than light dust.”

passage.zh: 后来我回故乡去，才知道一些较为详细的事。爱农先是什么事也没得做，因为大家讨厌他。他很困难，但还喝酒，是朋友请他的。他已经很少和人们来往，常见的只剩下几个后来认识的较为年青的人了，然而他们似乎也不愿意多听他的牢骚，以为不如讲笑话有趣。
passage.en: Later, when I went back to my home town, I learned some details. At first Ainong could find no work at all, because everyone disliked him. He was in great difficulty, but still drank; his friends treated him. He seldom had much to do with people any more; the only ones he often saw were a few rather younger men he had got to know later, and even they seemed unwilling to listen much to his complaints, thinking jokes more amusing.

passage.zh: “也许明天就收到一个电报，拆开来一看，是鲁迅来叫我的。”他时常这样说。
passage.en: “Perhaps tomorrow I'll get a telegram, and when I open it, it'll be Lu Xun sending for me.” He often said this.

passage.zh: 一天，几个新的朋友约他坐船去看戏，回来已过夜半，又是大风雨，他醉着，却偏要到船舷上去小解。大家劝阻他，也不听，自己说是不会掉下去的。但他掉下去了，虽然能浮水，却从此不起来。
passage.en: One day some new friends invited him to go by boat to see an opera. By the time they came back it was past midnight, and there was a great storm of wind and rain. He was drunk, yet insisted on going to the side of the boat to relieve himself. Everyone tried to stop him, but he would not listen, saying he would not fall in. But he did fall in, and though he could swim, he never came up again.

passage.zh: 第二天打捞尸体，是在菱荡里找到的，直立着。
passage.en: The next day they dragged for the body, and found it in the water-chestnut pond, standing upright.

passage.zh: 我至今不明白他究竟是失足还是自杀。
passage.en: To this day I do not know whether he slipped or killed himself.

passage.zh: 他死后一无所有，遗下一个幼女和他的夫人。有几个人想集一点钱作他女孩将来的学费的基金，因为一经提议，即有族人来争这笔款的保管权，——其实还没有这笔款，——大家觉得无聊，便无形消散了。
passage.en: He left nothing when he died, except a young daughter and his wife. A few people thought of raising a little money as a fund for his daughter's future schooling, but as soon as it was proposed, members of his clan came forward to fight over the right to keep the money,—when in fact there was no money yet,—and everyone found it so senseless that the idea quietly came to nothing.

passage.zh: 现在不知他唯一的女儿景况如何？倘在上学，中学已该毕业了罢。
passage.en: I wonder now how his only daughter is getting on? If she is at school, she should have finished middle school by now, I suppose.

passage.zh: 十一月十八日。
passage.en: November 18.

names.en: Jo Shiki Rin (Japanese reading of Xu Xilin)

notes.zh: 这是“徐锡麟”三字的日语读音。日本报纸用罗马字转写，所以留学生们一时猜不出是哪三个汉字。
notes.en: This is the Japanese reading of the characters for Xu Xilin. The Japanese paper gave it in romanization, which is why the students could not at first tell which three characters were meant.

notes.zh: 清代一省的最高地方长官之一，掌管一省的民政与军务。
notes.en: In the Qing dynasty, one of the highest officials of a province, in charge of its civil and military affairs.

notes.zh: 清代已经取得道员资格、等待正式补缺的官员，常常被临时委派办理某项事务。
notes.en: A Qing official who already held the rank of circuit intendant but was still waiting for a substantive post. Such men were often given temporary assignments in the meantime.
An old word for travel expenses.

notes.zh: 原指失去主家的武士，近代泛指没有固定职业、四处活动的日本人。其中有些人与中国革命者往来，替他们奔走办事。
notes.en: Originally samurai without a lord. In modern times the word meant Japanese men without fixed occupation, some of whom associated with Chinese revolutionaries and ran errands for them.

notes.zh: 绍兴一带定时往返于乡镇与城里的载客船，是当地常见的交通方式。
notes.en: In the Shaoxing area, a boat that carried passengers on a regular run between the villages and the town. It was a common way to travel locally.

notes.zh: 即海关，负责检查入境行李、征收关税。
notes.en: The customs office, which inspected incoming luggage and collected duties.

notes.zh: 旧时缠足女子穿的鞋，鞋底弯曲如弓，形制很小。
notes.en: Tiny shoes with arched soles worn by women with bound feet.

notes.zh: 这里的“鸟”是旧白话里的粗口，用作骂人的话。
notes.en: Here niao is a coarse curse word from old vernacular Chinese.

notes.zh: “匪刑”即“非刑”，指法外的、不合常规的残酷刑罚。
notes.en: That is, cruel punishment outside the law.

notes.zh: 指缠足的女子改穿大鞋，装作天足（未缠的脚）的样子。从鲁迅这句话看，缠足女子到了东京，通常要这样做。
notes.en: That is, a woman with bound feet would wear larger shoes and pass as having natural, unbound feet. Lu Xun's remark implies that a woman with bound feet would be expected to do this once in Tokyo.

notes.zh: 辛亥革命时，革命派称推翻清朝统治、恢复汉人政权为“光复”。
notes.en: During the 1911 Revolution, revolutionaries called the overthrow of Qing rule a restoration of Han rule.

notes.zh: 绍兴一带农夫常戴的毡帽。
notes.en: The felt hat commonly worn by peasants in the Shaoxing area.

notes.zh: 旧式学校里管理学生纪律和日常事务的职员。后文又作“学监”，指的是同一职务。
notes.en: A staff member in charge of student discipline and daily affairs at an old-style school. Paragraph 46 calls it xuejian, which is the same post.

notes.zh: 这是鲁迅的戏称。“绿林”指占山聚众的人，“绿林大学出身”是说王金发出身绿林。
notes.en: A joke by Lu Xun. The greenwood stands for outlaw bands, so the phrase means that Wang Jinfa came from the outlaw world.

notes.zh: 民国初年主张尊孔、把孔子学说定为国教的团体。
notes.en: A group of the early Republic that promoted the veneration of Confucius and wanted Confucianism made the state religion.

notes.zh: 北洋军阀，鲁迅写作此文时控制东南数省。他曾下令禁止美术学校使用裸体模特儿，鲁迅这里是在借题讥讽。
notes.en: A northern warlord who controlled several southeastern provinces when Lu Xun wrote this essay. He had ordered art schools to stop using nude models, and Lu Xun is mocking him here.

notes.zh: 旧时同乡在京城或其他城市设立的馆舍，供同乡寄居、聚会。
notes.en: A hostel set up in the capital or another city by people from the same home region, where they could lodge and meet.
A shallow pond where water chestnuts grow.

continue.zh: 《范爱农》是《朝花夕拾》的最后一篇正文，其后是作者的《后记》，补谈前面几篇涉及的旧图画和掌故。
continue.en: “Fan Ainong” is the last essay in Dawn Blossoms Plucked at Dusk. It is followed by the author’s Afterword, which returns to the old pictures and lore mentioned in the earlier essays.

selection.why: 这是一篇完整的回忆散文，人物从“可恶”到相知、再到潦倒而死，转折鲜明，又一层层揭开。东京同乡会上，范爱农冷冷一句“杀的杀掉了，死的死掉了，还发什么屁电报呢”；故乡重逢时，两人同时喊出对方的名字；光复那天，他戴着毡帽，露出从来没有见过的笑容；最后他在菱荡里被找到时“直立着”。这些细节写出了一个耿介、孤傲又无处容身的人。鲁迅的笔调也值得细读：他自嘲当年在横滨“摇头”，讽刺王都督与报馆的“股本”，在人物死后只说“我至今不明白”，克制而沉痛。全文篇幅适中，正好整篇呈现，不必删节。
selection.standalone: 开头是东京客店里众人早晨看报，读到徐锡麟刺杀恩铭的电报，读者随即进入留日学生群情激愤的场面，范爱农在争执中登场。结尾写到他死后，遗下的幼女无人照料，作者问一句“现在不知他唯一的女儿景况如何”，再记下写作日期，全文自然收束。
context_needed: 作者鲁迅清末在日本东京留学，文中的同乡多是浙江绍兴人。
徐锡麟（字伯荪）是绍兴人，1907年在安庆刺杀安徽巡抚恩铭，事败被杀；同年秋瑾在绍兴遇害。范爱农是徐锡麟的学生。
1911年武昌起义后各地相继“光复”，脱离清廷；绍兴光复后，王金发带兵从杭州进城，做了绍兴的都督。
文中的“子英”“德清”“季茀”都是作者的同乡友人，作者只写了字或名，没有详细交代他们的身份。

review.reading: 全文照录，从报上的电报、同乡会争执，写到故乡重逢、光复后的绍兴和菱荡，叙事连贯，冷嘲与悲凉交替，很有吸引力。译文总体忠实流畅，“似乎”“也许”“大约”等限定和鲁迅的反讽语气都保留了下来。主要需补上“徐伯荪即徐锡麟”这一指代，并删去两三条注释中原文不支持的说法。

issues.problem: 正文第4、7、21段等处多称“徐伯荪”，导读和注释都只用“徐锡麟”，没有说明两者是同一人。读者读到“去接徐伯荪的家属”“他是徐伯荪的学生”时，会以为是另一个人，“师母”也就跟着弄不清是谁。另外，“徐锡麟和秋瑾都是浙江绍兴人”中秋瑾的籍贯原文不能支持，而秋瑾的出生地和祖籍说法不一，按规则7宜改成原文能支持的“在绍兴遇害”。
issues.proposed: 《范爱农》是鲁迅回忆性散文集《朝花夕拾》的最后一篇，作于1926年。这里选录全文。文章从1907年的一桩大案写起：徐锡麟（字伯荪，文中常称“徐伯荪”）在安徽刺杀巡抚恩铭，秋瑾随后在绍兴遇害。徐锡麟是浙江绍兴人，当时鲁迅也是在日本东京留学的绍兴学生。范爱农是徐锡麟的学生，在同乡会上与鲁迅针锋相对。几年后两人在故乡绍兴重逢，随后经历了辛亥革命，也看到革命之后的绍兴是什么样子。之所以选这一篇，是因为鲁迅写人很少直接下判断，他把自己当年的误会、偏见和惭愧都写了进来。全篇语气在冷嘲与悲凉之间来回转换，人物的处境就从这些细节里显出来。读的时候可以留意文中几次“摇头”和“电报”前后怎样呼应。

issues.problem: 与中文导读同样的问题：英文译文第4、7、21、24段称 Xu Bosun 和 our teacher's wife，导读只说 Xu Xilin，英文读者无法把两者对上。秋瑾籍贯也应同步改为原文能支持的说法。另外 embarrassment 比原文“惭愧”轻，宜作 shame。
issues.proposed: “Fan Ainong” is the last essay in Lu Xun’s memoir collection Dawn Blossoms Plucked at Dusk, written in 1926. It is given here in full. The essay begins with a famous case of 1907: Xu Xilin (courtesy name Bosun, and often called Xu Bosun in the essay) assassinated Enming, the governor of Anhui, and Qiu Jin was executed soon afterwards in Shaoxing. Xu came from Shaoxing in Zhejiang, and Lu Xun was then a Shaoxing student in Tokyo. Fan Ainong, a former student of Xu Xilin, clashes with Lu Xun at a meeting of their fellow provincials. Years later the two meet again in Shaoxing, live through the 1911 Revolution, and see what the town becomes after it. We chose this piece because Lu Xun rarely passes judgment outright. He includes his own misunderstandings, prejudices and shame, and the tone moves between dry irony and sorrow. Readers may watch how the head-shaking and the telegrams echo across the essay.

issues.problem: “在鞋里塞上填充物”和“当时到日本的中国女性常常这样做”都是原文不支持的说法。原文只有鲁迅一句“到东京就要假装大脚”。
issues.proposed: 指缠足的女子改穿大鞋，装作天足（未缠的脚）的样子。从鲁迅这句话看，缠足女子到了东京，通常要这样做。

issues.problem: “黑色”和“后来常被人当作绍兴乡下人的标志”原文不支持。原文只说“农夫常用的毡帽”。
issues.proposed: 绍兴一带农夫常戴的毡帽。

issues.problem: 孙传芳下令禁止美术学校使用裸体模特儿一事，超出原文和“确定无疑的基本事实”的范围。此事有史料可查，也有助于读懂这里的讥讽，但需核实后保留，或者改得更简略。

edits.from: 《范爱农》是鲁迅回忆性散文集《朝花夕拾》的最后一篇，作于1926年。这里选录全文。文章从1907年的一桩大案写起：徐锡麟（字伯荪，文中常称“徐伯荪”）在安徽刺杀巡抚恩铭，秋瑾随后在绍兴遇害。徐锡麟是浙江绍兴人，当时鲁迅也是在日本东京留学的绍兴学生。范爱农是徐锡麟的学生，在同乡会上与鲁迅针锋相对。几年后两人在故乡绍兴重逢，随后经历了辛亥革命，也看到革命之后的绍兴是什么样子。之所以选这一篇，是因为鲁迅写人很少直接下判断，他把自己当年的误会、偏见和惭愧都写了进来。全篇语气在冷嘲与悲凉之间来回转换，人物的处境就从这些细节里显出来。读的时候可以留意文中几次“摇头”和“电报”前后怎样呼应。

edits.from: “Fan Ainong” is the last essay in Lu Xun’s memoir collection Dawn Blossoms Plucked at Dusk, written in 1926. It is given here in full. The essay begins with a famous case of 1907: Xu Xilin (courtesy name Bosun, and often called Xu Bosun in the essay) assassinated Enming, the governor of Anhui, and Qiu Jin was executed soon afterwards in Shaoxing. Xu came from Shaoxing in Zhejiang, and Lu Xun was then a Shaoxing student in Tokyo. Fan Ainong, a former student of Xu Xilin, clashes with Lu Xun at a meeting of their fellow provincials. Years later the two meet again in Shaoxing, live through the 1911 Revolution, and see what the town becomes after it. We chose this piece because Lu Xun rarely passes judgment outright. He includes his own misunderstandings, prejudices and shame, and the tone moves between dry irony and sorrow. Readers may watch how the head-shaking and the telegrams echo across the essay.

review.reading: 两个问题紧扣文本、开放而不预设答案，参考角度也标明了“一种读法”；但其中一处引文错位，结尾一句略带说教，修正后能更好地留给读者自己判断。

issues.problem: 引文对应错了。P10“无理，倒也并非无理的”评的是 P9 范爱农那句“何必推举呢？自然是主张发电的人啰”，不是 P6 的“屁电报”一句。参考角度把这句评语接在 P6 后面，等于把原文没说的话算到鲁迅头上：好像他承认反对发电本身“并非无理”。
issues.proposed: 文中有两处“电报”可以对照。东京同乡会上，范爱农说：“杀的杀掉了，死的死掉了，还发什么屁电报呢。”（P6）鲁迅当时认定他冷漠怕事。多年后，穷困中的范爱农常说：“也许明天就收到一个电报，拆开来一看，是鲁迅来叫我的。”（P50）当年他看不上的电报，后来成了他的盼望。一种可能的理解是：他看轻的未必是情义，而是空泛的表态；他自己盼着的，是一个具体的人来叫他。两人当初凭会上的几句冷话、税关上的一次摇头（P21）互相厌恶，后来却成了朋友，或许可以让人想想第一印象能说明多少。不过原文没有交代范爱农当年反对发电的真正理由，这只是一种读法。

issues.problem: 与中文同样的引文错位：“unreasonable, and yet not without reason”（P10）评的是 P9 关于推举拟稿人的话，不是 P6 关于电报的话。
issues.proposed: Two telegrams in the essay are worth setting side by side. At the Tokyo meeting, Fan says: “The killed are killed, the dead are dead. What’s the use of a damned telegram?” (P6) At the time Lu Xun took this for coldness and cowardice. Years later, poor and isolated, Fan would often say: “Maybe tomorrow I’ll get a telegram, open it, and find it’s Lu Xun sending for me.” (P50) The telegram he once scorned became the thing he hoped for. One possible reading is that what he scorned was not loyalty but empty gestures, and what he longed for was a particular person calling him. The two men first disliked each other over a few cold remarks at a meeting and one shake of the head at customs (P21), yet later became friends. That may make us wonder how much a first impression really tells us. Still, the text never gives Fan’s real reason for opposing the telegram, so this is only one way to read it.

issues.problem: “这也提醒我们……容易看错人”写成了普遍教训，接近说教，也没有说明适用边界。中文还比英文“hints at”语气更重，篇幅也略超 250 字。上面的修改已改为“或许可以让人想想”，并略作压缩。
issues.proposed: 同 Q1 的修改文字。

issues.problem: “起因是横滨码头上的一次摇头”是范爱农在 P18–P20 里的说法，问题里写成了编辑认定的事实。原文还说讨厌鲁迅的不只他一人（“不但我，我们”），而且摇头发生在税关检查时。
issues.proposed: 鲁迅在东京时认定范爱农“冷”“可恶”。多年后范爱农告诉他：自己和同船来的那群人一向讨厌他，因为在横滨税关上看见他摇了头。两人对彼此的成见各自是怎样形成的？重逢以后，又是什么让他们成了常在一起喝酒的朋友？

issues.problem: 与中文同：讨厌的起因是范爱农的说法，讨厌他的是“我们”一群人，摇头发生在税关。
issues.proposed: In Tokyo, Lu Xun decided that Fan Ainong was “cold” and “detestable.” Years later Fan told him that he and the others who came over on the same boat had disliked him all along, because they saw him shake his head at the Yokohama customs. en: In Tokyo, Lu Xun decided that Fan Ainong was “cold” and “detestable.” Years later he learned that Fan had disliked him all along, and that it began with a shake of the head on the dock at Yokohama. How did each man form his prejudice about the other? And after they met again, what turned them into friends who drank together?

Writing about Fan’s death, Lu Xun first says “I suspected he had killed himself,” then says the news felt “utterly reliable, though there was no proof,” and finally writes “To this day I do not know whether he slipped or killed himself.” Why does he not reach a conclusion? How do this wavering and uncertainty shape the way you feel the ending?

angle.zh: 文中有两处“电报”可以对照。东京同乡会上，范爱农说：“杀的杀掉了，死的死掉了，还发什么屁电报呢。”鲁迅当时认定他冷漠怕事。多年后，穷困中的范爱农常说：“也许明天就收到一个电报，拆开来一看，是鲁迅来叫我的。”当年他看不上的电报，后来成了他的盼望。一种可能的理解是：他看轻的未必是情义，而是空泛的表态；他自己盼着的，是一个具体的人来叫他。两人当初凭会上的几句冷话、税关上的一次摇头互相厌恶，后来却成了朋友，或许可以让人想想第一印象能说明多少。不过原文没有交代范爱农当年反对发电的真正理由，这只是一种读法。
angle.en: Two telegrams in the essay are worth setting side by side. At the Tokyo meeting, Fan says: “The killed are killed, the dead are dead. What’s the use of a damned telegram?” At the time Lu Xun took this for coldness and cowardice. Years later, poor and isolated, Fan would often say: “Maybe tomorrow I’ll get a telegram, open it, and find it’s Lu Xun sending for me.” The telegram he once scorned became the thing he hoped for. One possible reading is that what he scorned was not loyalty but empty gestures, and what he longed for was a particular person calling him. The two men first disliked each other over a few cold remarks at a meeting and one shake of the head at customs, yet later became friends. That may make us wonder how much a first impression really tells us. Still, the text never gives Fan’s real reason for opposing the telegram, so this is only one way to read it.
